facts.claim: The project 'Us vs. Them' is hosted at https://github.com/eighttrigrams/us-vs-them and provides diff-based line-level provenance for text under agentic editing, using git history to distinguish human from AI authorship without inline markup.
The Hacker News discussion of 'Us vs. Them' received 29 points.
The project is described as a CLI/library for line-level provenance in text edited by humans and agents, using version history to estimate which ranges are human-written versus machine-generated.
On AgentDish, the tool received a score of 78, with strengths in clear presentation and weaknesses around undocumented algorithm limits and packaging.

The ICLR 2026 paper 'EditLens' proposes lightweight similarity metrics and a regression model to quantify the magnitude of AI editing in text, achieving 94.7% F1 on binary and 90.4% F1 on ternary classification for distinguishing human, AI-generated, and mixed writing.
EditLens has implications for authorship attribution, education, and policy.

Orca tracks provenance on every line an agent touches, rendering AI-originated lines with gutter markers in its diff viewer; attribution is local to Orca and not committed to git, and human edits on top of AI code flip attribution back to human.
Orca's line-level attribution aids security audits and faster reviews.

agentdiff hooks into major AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Windsurf, OpenCode, Gemini) and writes permanent, commit-scoped attribution records capturing agent name, model, prompt excerpt, and exact line ranges.
agentdiff provides git-blame-style line-level attribution and stats, and is installable globally via a configure command.

Us vs. Them, Orca, agentdiff, and EditLens all address the problem of distinguishing human from AI contributions at a line or range level in text or code, but they take different approaches: git-history analysis (Us vs. Them), local gutter markers (Orca), commit-scoped agent records (agentdiff), and similarity/regression metrics (EditLens).

angles.thesis: Git-history-based provenance like Us vs. Them has a fundamental blind spot: it can only operate on what was committed, meaning it is trivially defeated by a human who squashes, amends, or copies AI output into a fresh commit.
angles.whyItFits: This is a concrete technical critique from someone who thinks about trade-offs in tooling, not hype. It engages the craft of building provenance systems rather than just celebrating them.
evidenceNeeded: Evidence that git-history approaches rely on commit granularity (inferred from src_c54bc1, src_f022fe)
General knowledge of git workflows like squash and amend
angles.noveltyNote: No recent posts exist, but this is a straightforward technical limitation argument that someone familiar with git will arrive at quickly. The specific framing around 'defeat by squash' is less obvious.

angles.thesis: The more interesting problem is not distinguishing human from AI text — it is that once an agent edits a line, that line is no longer purely either, and binary provenance labels actively mislead.
angles.whyItFits: Matches the belief that AI products should solve concrete problems, and the audience of engineers tired of hype. This reframes the whole category from a classification problem to a blending problem.
evidenceNeeded: EditLens paper's ternary classification (src_979180) shows the field already recognizes a 'mixed' category
Orca's behavior of flipping attribution on human edit (src_e969a1) demonstrates the binary assumption in practice
angles.noveltyNote: No recent posts exist. EditLens explicitly addresses ternary classification, but the argument that binary labels are actively harmful rather than just incomplete is a sharper claim.

angles.thesis: The divergence between Orca (local, ephemeral markers) and agentdiff (permanent, commit-scoped records) reveals that the real product decision in provenance tools is whether attribution belongs to the artifact or to the review environment — and there is no single right answer.
angles.whyItFits: Speaks directly to product decisions, trade-offs, and the belief that good UX matters more than features. The audience of engineers and product people will recognize this as a genuine design tension.
evidenceNeeded: Orca keeps attribution local and not in git (src_e969a1)
Us vs. Them uses existing git history rather than adding new metadata (src_c54bc1)
angles.noveltyNote: No recent posts exist, but comparing tools in a category is the most obvious angle. The specific framing around 'artifact vs. review environment' is a useful lens.

angles.thesis: The four approaches to AI provenance — git-history inference, gutter markers, commit-scoped agent records, and similarity regression — each make a different bet about where the ground truth lives, and that bet determines everything else about the tool.
angles.whyItFits: Fits the 'plain explanation' slot for an audience that wants to understand the landscape before forming opinions. Avoids hype by mapping the design space rather than picking winners.
evidenceNeeded: Us vs. Them uses git history (src_c54bc1, src_f022fe)
angles.noveltyNote: No recent posts exist. A taxonomy-of-approaches post is a common format, but the 'where does ground truth live' framing gives it a sharper thesis.

angles.thesis: If provenance tools become standard, do we end up with a world where the 'human-written' label becomes a status signal — and what happens when that status is gamed the way SEO gamed PageRank?
angles.whyItFits: The audience of engineers and product people will recognize this as a second-order effect worth thinking about. It connects a technical topic to a broader pattern without being moralizing.
evidenceNeeded: General knowledge of how metrics become targets (Goodhart's law)
Evidence that provenance tools are being adopted (inferred from multiple tools emerging: src_b18586, src_e969a1, src_c54bc1)
The EditLens paper mentions policy implications (src_979180)
angles.noveltyNote: No recent posts exist, but 'metrics become targets' is a well-worn observation. The specific analogy to PageRank and SEO gives it a concrete shape.

angles.thesis: The fact that Us vs. Them scored 78 on AgentDish for 'clear presentation' but was dinged for undocumented algorithm limits is the whole story: provenance tools are easy to demo and hard to trust, and trust is the only thing that matters for this category.
angles.whyItFits: This is an opinionated take grounded in a specific data point, fitting the 62/100 opinionated scale and the preference for concrete observation over motivational advice.
evidenceNeeded: AgentDish score of 78 with strengths in clear presentation and weaknesses around undocumented algorithm limits (src_f022fe)

This is the actual product decision in provenance tools: does attribution belong to the artifact or to the review environment? I don't think there's a single right answer.

drafts.text: The split between Orca and agentdiff is a quiet but real design fork. One treats provenance as ephemeral review context — local markers, never committed. The other makes it a permanent record in git history. Same problem, two different beliefs about where attribution should live. That's the kind of trade-off worth watching.

drafts.text: Us vs. Them reconstructs provenance from git history after the fact. Orca and agentdiff capture it live — but disagree on whether it should be commit-scoped or local. The interesting thing is that all three approaches are shipping, and none of them agree on the right place for attribution to live. Good UX here might matter more than algorithmic accuracy.

src_e969a1 says Orca tracks provenance locally in its diff viewer, not committed to git; src_b18586 says agentdiff writes commit-scoped attribution records. The disagreement on commit-scoped vs. local is directly stated.

All three tools are described as existing/shipping, and they disagree on where attribution lives: Us vs. Them uses git history, Orca keeps it local, agentdiff commits it. The inference is reasonable from the sources.
